claim: Ten male rhesus macaque monkeys (5–11 kg) were used in this study.
source: Ten male rhesus macaque monkeys (5–11 kg) were used in this study.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the subjects.

claim: Three monkeys (BI, FG, and ST) were used for recording experiments.
source: Of these, three (BI, FG, and ST) were also used for recording, and one (ST) and two (BI and RI) for chemogenetic and pharmacological inactivation experiments, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing which monkeys were used for which experiments.

claim: Monkey ST was used for chemogenetic inactivation experiments.
source: Of these, three (BI, FG, and ST) were also used for recording, and one (ST) and two (BI and RI) for chemogenetic and pharmacological inactivation experiments, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Monkeys BI and RI were used for pharmacological inactivation experiments.
source: Of these, three (BI, FG, and ST) were also used for recording, and one (ST) and two (BI and RI) for chemogenetic and pharmacological inactivation experiments, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the National Institutes for Quantum and Radiological Science and Technology (11-1038-11).
source: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the National Institutes for Quantum and Radiological Science and Technology (11-1038-11) and by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Mental Health (Annual Report ZIAMH002619), and were in accordance with the Institute of Laboratory Animal Research Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Mental Health (Annual Report ZIAMH002619).
source: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the National Institutes for Quantum and Radiological Science and Technology (11-1038-11) and by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Mental Health (Annual Report ZIAMH002619), and were in accordance with the Institute of Laboratory Animal Research Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The experimental procedures were in accordance with the Institute of Laboratory Animal Research Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
source: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the National Institutes for Quantum and Radiological Science and Technology (11-1038-11) and by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Mental Health (Annual Report ZIAMH002619), and were in accordance with the Institute of Laboratory Animal Research Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Error rates in the delayed reward task were higher when a small reward size was expected.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the error rates were higher when a small reward size was expected, and for both reward sizes, the errors increased linearly as the expected delay duration increased.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1C with behavioral data.

claim: For both reward sizes, errors increased linearly as the expected delay duration increased.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the error rates were higher when a small reward size was expected, and for both reward sizes, the errors increased linearly as the expected delay duration increased.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1C with behavioral data.

claim: The pattern of averaged error rates was well described by the inverse relation with hyperbolic delay discounting (Equation 2) with R² = 0.96, 0.88, and 0.94 for monkeys BI, FG, and ST, respectively.
source: This pattern of the averaged error rates was well described by the inverse relation with hyperbolic delay discounting (Equation 2) (R2 = 0.96, 0.88, and 0.94 for monkeys BI, FG, and ST, respectively; Figure 1C, solid lines).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² values and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The exponential discounting model explained the majority of cases (7/10 monkeys, R² > 0.9).
source: The exponential discounting model (Equation 3) also explained the majority of the cases (7/10 monkeys, R2 > 0.9; e.g., Figure 1C, dotted curves for monkeys BI and ST) well.
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Leave-one-out cross-validation analysis confirmed that the hyperbolic model fitted the error rates significantly better than exponential function for all three monkeys as well as for seven additional monkeys (p<0.05).
source: Consistent with previous results (Minamimoto et al., 2009), leave-one-out cross-validation analysis confirmed that the hyperbolic model fitted the error rates significantly better than exponential function for all three monkeys as well as for seven additional monkeys (p<0.05; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous work and reference to Materials and methods.

claim: Reaction times were shorter for larger rewards (two-way ANOVA; p<0.001, 8/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST).
source: The reaction times also covaried with both reward size and reward delay; reaction times were shorter for larger rewards (two-way ANOVA; p<0.001, 8/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST) and shorter delays (p<0.001, 9/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reaction times were shorter for shorter delays (p<0.001, 9/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST).
source: The reaction times also covaried with both reward size and reward delay; reaction times were shorter for larger rewards (two-way ANOVA; p<0.001, 8/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST) and shorter delays (p<0.001, 9/10 monkeys including monkeys BI, FG, and ST, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant effect of forthcoming reward size or delay duration on the duration of gazing at the cue was found (two-way ANOVA; main effect of reward size, effect size η² = 0.004; main effect of delay, η² = 0.002; reward size × delay, η² = 0.003).
source: Although the monkeys were not required to fixate during the task, they usually gazed at the cue during the cue period. We did not find any significant effect of forthcoming reward size or delay duration on the duration of gazing at the cue (two-way ANOVA; main effect of reward size, effect size η2 = 0.004; main effect of delay, η2 = 0.002; reward size × delay, η2 = 0.003) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The monkeys adjusted their motivation of action based on the temporally discounted value, which forms a hyperbolic relationship between expected size and delay of forthcoming reward.
source: Together, these results suggest that the monkeys adjusted their motivation of action based on the temporally discounted value, which forms a hyperbolic relationship between expected size and delay of forthcoming reward.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral data presented.

claim: 150 presumed projection neurons (i.e., phasically active neurons) were recorded from dCDh.
source: Specifically, we focused on dCDh and recorded the activity of 150 presumed projection neurons (i.e., phasically active neurons; see Materials and methods) (Figure 1D), while the monkeys performed the delayed reward task.
evidence: Stated in text and recording locations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Most of the neurons (n = 118) significantly increased their activity around more than one of three task phases: cue, release, and/or reward (p<0.05, χ² test).
source: Most of the neurons (n = 118) significantly increased their activity around more than one of three task phases: cue (immediately after cue appearance), release (at the time of bar release), and/or reward (at the time of reward delivery) (Figure 2A–C; p<0.05, χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The proportion of cue-responsive neurons (100/150) was significantly larger than that of release-responsive neurons (49/150; p<0.01, χ² test).
source: The cue response was the most prominent activity of dCDh neurons during the task (Figure 2A,C); the proportion of cue-responsive neurons (100/150) was significantly larger than that of release-responsive neurons (49/150; p<0.01, χ2 test) and reward-responsive neurons (Figure 2D; 49/150; p<0.0001, χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The proportion of cue-responsive neurons (100/150) was significantly larger than that of reward-responsive neurons (49/150; p<0.0001, χ² test).
source: The cue response was the most prominent activity of dCDh neurons during the task (Figure 2A,C); the proportion of cue-responsive neurons (100/150) was significantly larger than that of release-responsive neurons (49/150; p<0.01, χ2 test) and reward-responsive neurons (Figure 2D; 49/150; p<0.0001, χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A significant regression coefficient for DV (p<0.05, t-test) was found in 27 of 100 cue-responsive neurons (11, 6, and 10 in monkeys BI, FG, and ST, respectively).
source: A significant regression coefficient for DV (p<0.05, t-test) was found in 27 of 100 cue-responsive neurons (11, 6, and 10 in monkeys BI, FG, and ST, respectively); 18 and 9 exhibited positive and negative correlations, respectively.
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and specific numbers for each monkey.

claim: 18 DV-coding neurons exhibited positive correlations and 9 exhibited negative correlations.
source: A significant regression coefficient for DV (p<0.05, t-test) was found in 27 of 100 cue-responsive neurons (11, 6, and 10 in monkeys BI, FG, and ST, respectively); 18 and 9 exhibited positive and negative correlations, respectively.
evidence: Stated in text describing the directionality of DV correlations.

claim: A similar number of neurons (n = 25) showed a significant DV relation when estimating using the exponential function (Equation 3).
source: The result did not seem to depend on the shape of DV function: a similar number of neurons showed a significant DV relation when estimating using the exponential function (Equation 3; n = 25).
evidence: Stated in text comparing hyperbolic and exponential models.

claim: Significant DV relation was relatively minor in release-related (5/49) and reward responses (3/49).
source: By contrast, significant DV relation was relatively minor in release-related (5/49) and reward responses (3/49).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers.

claim: Only three neurons showed a significant exclusive effect of size on cue response.
source: We found that only three and four neurons showed a significant exclusive effect of size or delay on their cue response, respectively (Figure 4A,B, blue and green).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Only four neurons showed a significant exclusive effect of delay on cue response.
source: We found that only three and four neurons showed a significant exclusive effect of size or delay on their cue response, respectively (Figure 4A,B, blue and green).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: For 19 neurons, DV had a significant effect on the cue response.
source: In contrast, for 19 and 5 neurons, DV and both delay and size had a significant effect on the cue response, respectively (Figure 4A,B, red and pink), the proportions of which were significantly larger than that of neurons by chance coding both delay and reward size (p<0.01; χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: For 5 neurons, both delay and size had a significant effect on the cue response.
source: In contrast, for 19 and 5 neurons, DV and both delay and size had a significant effect on the cue response, respectively (Figure 4A,B, red and pink), the proportions of which were significantly larger than that of neurons by chance coding both delay and reward size (p<0.01; χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The proportions of neurons with DV effects were significantly larger than that of neurons by chance coding both delay and reward size (p<0.01; χ² test).
source: In contrast, for 19 and 5 neurons, DV and both delay and size had a significant effect on the cue response, respectively (Figure 4A,B, red and pink), the proportions of which were significantly larger than that of neurons by chance coding both delay and reward size (p<0.01; χ2 test).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test.

claim: The effect size of DV rose from 100 ms after cue onset, reaching a peak at 750 ms after the cue.
source: On average, the effect size rose from 100 ms after cue onset, reaching a peak at 750 ms after the cue (red curve, Figure 5C).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The effect size of DV gradually decreased to the bar release after reaching its peak.
source: Thereafter, it gradually decreased to the bar release (Figure 5D).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A few neurons (n = 5) also signaled DV around bar release.
source: The effect size did not become 0, indicating that a few neurons (n = 5) also signaled DV around bar release.
evidence: Stated in text with specific number.

claim: The majority of DV-coding neurons (17 of 22) were modulated differentially by DV depending on whether the monkey performed correctly or not.
source: We found that the majority of DV-coding neurons (17 of 22) were modulated differentially by DV depending on whether the monkey performed correctly or not (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), supporting the idea that this population of neurons is involved in motivational processes.
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: As the normalized cumulative reward (Rcum) increased, the overall error rate in each combination of reward size and delay also increased.
source: As the normalized cumulative reward (Rcum) increased, the overall error rate in each combination of reward size and delay also increased (Figure 6A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The error rates were well explained by Equation 4 for each individual monkey (R² = 0.89 ± 0.06; mean ± sem).
source: The error rates were well explained by Equation 4 for each individual monkey (R2 = 0.89 ± 0.06; mean ± sem) as well as for the average across nine monkeys (R2 = 0.98, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² values and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The error rates were well explained by Equation 4 for the average across nine monkeys (R² = 0.98).
source: The error rates were well explained by Equation 4 for each individual monkey (R2 = 0.89 ± 0.06; mean ± sem) as well as for the average across nine monkeys (R2 = 0.98, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² value and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The motivational value of reward decreased at a rate of more than 15% (16%, 33%, and 17% for BI, FG, and ST, respectively) in a single recording session (i.e., 120 trials).
source: The satiation effect, F(Rcum) (Figure 6C), indicated that the motivational value of reward decreased at a rate of more than 15% (16%, 33%, and 17% for BI, FG, and ST, respectively) in a single recording session (i.e., 120 trials) according to the number of average success trials in a daily session.
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentages and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The normalized mean discharge rate of cue responses for each reward condition did not significantly change between the first and second halves in 18 positive DV-coding neurons (repeated-measures two-way ANOVA; main effect of trial type, F(5, 119) = 16.8, p<10⁻⁸; main effect of satiation, F(1, 119) = 1.7, p=0.29).
source: Similarly, the normalized mean discharge rate of cue responses for each reward condition did not significantly change between the first and second halves in 18 positive DV-coding neurons (repeated-measures two-way ANOVA; main effect of trial type, F(5, 119) = 16.8, p<10−8; main effect of satiation, F(1, 119) = 1.7, p=0.29; Figure 6E).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A significant satiation effect was not found in any of the cue-responsive dCDh neurons (97/100) except for three non-DV-coding neurons.
source: Additional neuron-by-neuron analysis using a multiple linear regression model (Equation 9) demonstrated that a significant satiation effect was not found in any of the cue-responsive dCDh neurons (97/100) except for three non-DV-coding neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: dCDh neurons encode the expected temporally discounted value in their cue response without reflecting internal physiological drive.
source: Therefore, dCDh neurons encode the expected temporally discounted value in their cue response without reflecting internal physiological drive.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the satiation analysis.

claim: Bilateral inactivation of dCDh resulted in a significant shift in error rate patterns with respect to reward size and delay in all three monkeys.
source: Both pharmacological and chemogenetic inactivation resulted in a significant shift in error rate patterns with respect to reward size and delay in all three monkeys (Figure 7D, left); the behavioral patterns were idiosyncratic across the monkeys, but they were generally not in accordance with the temporal discounting model (i.e., Equation 2; R2 = 0.41, 0.19, and 0.76, for monkeys BI, RI, and ST, respectively).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² values and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The behavioral patterns after inactivation were generally not in accordance with the temporal discounting model (R² = 0.41, 0.19, and 0.76, for monkeys BI, RI, and ST, respectively).
source: Both pharmacological and chemogenetic inactivation resulted in a significant shift in error rate patterns with respect to reward size and delay in all three monkeys (Figure 7D, left); the behavioral patterns were idiosyncratic across the monkeys, but they were generally not in accordance with the temporal discounting model (i.e., Equation 2; R2 = 0.41, 0.19, and 0.76, for monkeys BI, RI, and ST, respectively).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² values and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The error rate pattern following vehicle injection remained well explained by the model (R² > 0.86).
source: By contrast, the error rate pattern following vehicle injection remained well explained by the model (Figure 7D, right; R2 > 0.86).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² value and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Inactivation did not produce statistically significant changes in the overall error rates (inactivation vs. control; two-way ANOVA for treatment × reward condition; main effect of treatment, F(1, 2) = 13.6, p=0.07; interaction, F(5, 164) = 2.1, p=0.07).
source: Despite changing error patterns, inactivation did not produce statistically significant changes in the overall error rates (inactivation vs. control; two-way ANOVA for treatment × reward condition; main effect of treatment, F(1, 2) = 13.6, p=0.07; interaction, F(5, 164) = 2.1, p=0.07).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis.

claim: The total reward earned during the task was unchanged in each monkey (inactivation vs. control; Brunner–Munzel test, p>0.18).
source: Apart from the error rates, the inactivation did not affect other behavioral parameters. The total reward earned during the task was unchanged in each monkey (inactivation vs. control; Brunner–Munzel test, p>0.18).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test.

claim: There was no significant effect of treatment on reaction time in two monkeys (two-way ANOVA, effect size of treatment: η² < 0.01, monkeys BI and RI).
source: There was no significant effect of treatment on reaction time in two monkeys (two-way ANOVA, effect size of treatment: η2 < 0.01, monkeys BI and RI) but a moderate effect of treatment in monkey ST (η2 = 0.06) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a moderate effect of treatment on reaction time in monkey ST (η² = 0.06).
source: There was no significant effect of treatment on reaction time in two monkeys (two-way ANOVA, effect size of treatment: η2 < 0.01, monkeys BI and RI) but a moderate effect of treatment in monkey ST (η2 = 0.06) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Type of error (i.e., releasing too early or too late) was unaffected by inactivation (main effect of treatment, F(1,26) = 1.07, p=0.31).
source: Type of error (i.e., releasing too early or too late) was unaffected by inactivation (main effect of treatment, F(1,26) = 1.07, p=0.31).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of releases depended on reward condition (main effect of reward condition, F(5, 143) = 25.22, p<0.001), but there was no significant main effect of treatment (two-way ANOVA, treatment, F(1, 143) = 2.90, p=0.09) or interaction (F(5, 143) = 0.42, p=0.83).
source: The monkeys touched and released the bar several times during the delay period, even though the delay time was not shortened. The number of releases depended on reward condition (main effect of reward condition, F(5, 143) = 25.22, p<0.001), but there was no significant main effect of treatment (two-way ANOVA, treatment, F(1, 143) = 2.90, p=0.09) or interaction (F(5, 143) = 0.42, p=0.83).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis.

claim: The duration of gazing at the cue was slightly but not significantly longer during muscimol inactivation (t-test, p=0.063).
source: The duration of gazing at the cue was slightly but not significantly longer during muscimol inactivation (t-test, p=0.063, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The bilateral inactivation of dCDh did not cause impairments in overall motivation, motor, or anticipatory behavior.
source: Together, the bilateral inactivation of dCDh did not cause impairments in overall motivation, motor, or anticipatory behavior.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral measures.

claim: Bootstrap analysis revealed that, compared to baseline data, inactivation, but not control, caused significant deviations in the error rate patterns away from the temporal discounting model in all monkeys (p<0.05).
source: Bootstrap analysis revealed that, compared to baseline data, inactivation, but not control, caused significant deviations in the error rate patterns away from the temporal discounting model in all monkeys (p<0.05, Figure 7E, red line), suggesting that dCDh silencing distorted normal motivational value processing based on the integration between reward size and delay.
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: dCDh silencing distorted normal motivational value processing based on the integration between reward size and delay.
source: Bootstrap analysis revealed that, compared to baseline data, inactivation, but not control, caused significant deviations in the error rate patterns away from the temporal discounting model in all monkeys (p<0.05, Figure 7E, red line), suggesting that dCDh silencing distorted normal motivational value processing based on the integration between reward size and delay.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on bootstrap analysis.

claim: Pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of bilateral dCDh did not alter the pattern of the error rate in the reward-size task; in both cases they remained to be well explained by the model (R² > 0.7).
source: Pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of bilateral dCDh did not alter the pattern of the error rate in this task; in both cases they remained to be well explained by the model (R2 > 0.7) (Figure 8C) and were equally well compared with the baseline data (p>0.15, bootstrap significance test; Figure 8D).
evidence: Stated in text with specific R² value and shown in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: The error rate patterns in the reward-size task after inactivation were equally well compared with the baseline data (p>0.15, bootstrap significance test).
source: Pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of bilateral dCDh did not alter the pattern of the error rate in this task; in both cases they remained to be well explained by the model (R2 > 0.7) (Figure 8C) and were equally well compared with the baseline data (p>0.15, bootstrap significance test; Figure 8D).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical test and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The inactivation did not change the overall error rates in the reward-size task (three-way ANOVA, treatment, F(1, 243) = 1.35, p=0.45).
source: The inactivation did not change the overall error rates (three-way ANOVA, treatment, F(1, 243) = 1.35, p=0.45) or the interactive effect with reward size on the error rates (treatment × size, F(3, 243) = 1.69, p=0.17).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis.

claim: The inactivation did not change the interactive effect with reward size on the error rates in the reward-size task (treatment × size, F(3, 243) = 1.69, p=0.17).
source: The inactivation did not change the overall error rates (three-way ANOVA, treatment, F(1, 243) = 1.35, p=0.45) or the interactive effect with reward size on the error rates (treatment × size, F(3, 243) = 1.69, p=0.17).
evidence: Stated in text with statistical analysis.

claim: dCDh activity is specifically involved in computing the motivational value based on delay discounting, rather than general motivational processes based on the integration of incentives and drive.
source: Overall, these results suggest that dCDh activity is specifically involved in computing the motivational value based on delay discounting, rather than general motivational processes based on the integration of incentives and drive.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the differential effects of inactivation on delayed reward vs. reward-size tasks.

claim: Temporal discounting was originally proposed to describe choice preferences for earlier smaller rewards rather than later larger rewards.
source: Temporal discounting was originally proposed to describe choice preferences for earlier smaller rewards rather than later larger rewards (Mazur, 1984; Mazur, 2001; Green and Myerson, 2004), implying that motivation and decision-making may share common brain processes.
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work.

claim: Motivation and decision-making may share common brain processes.
source: Temporal discounting was originally proposed to describe choice preferences for earlier smaller rewards rather than later larger rewards (Mazur, 1984; Mazur, 2001; Green and Myerson, 2004), implying that motivation and decision-making may share common brain processes.
evidence: Stated as an implication based on the concept of temporal discounting.

claim: Motivational processes consider internal drive for reward, such as hunger and thirst, integrating these two factors into motivational value.
source: Besides temporal discounting, motivational processes also consider internal drive for reward, such as hunger and thirst, integrating these two factors into motivational value (Toates, 1986; Berridge, 2004; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work.

claim: The basal ganglia is one of the major candidates as the neural systems mediating the computation of expected outcome value and transforming it into action.
source: One of the major candidates as the neural systems mediating the computation of expected outcome value and transforming it into action is the basal ganglia (Daw and Doya, 2006; Hikosaka et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work.

claim: The caudate nucleus (CD) plays an important role in motivational processing via signaling an expected outcome and monitoring action/outcome leading to future behavioral improvement.
source: Several lines of evidence based on electrophysiological studies have suggested that the caudate nucleus (CD) plays an important role in motivational processing via signaling an expected outcome and monitoring action/outcome leading to future behavioral improvement (Kawagoe et al., 1998; Cromwell and Schultz, 2003; Lau and Glimcher, 2008; Hori et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work.

claim: The dorsal part of the head of the CD (dCDh) is best situated to participate in temporal discounting processes because it receives strong convergent inputs from various frontal cortical areas including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and the supplementary eye field (SEF).
source: Especially, the dorsal part of the head of the CD (dCDh) is best situated to participate in temporal discounting processes because it receives strong convergent inputs from various frontal cortical areas including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and the supplementary eye field (SEF) (Haber et al., 1995; Haber et al., 2006), where neuronal activity is related to the expected amount or delay/proximity of rewards (Shidara and Richmond, 2002; Roesch and Olson, 2003; Roesch and Olson, 2005; Tsujimoto and Sawaguchi, 2005; Sohn and Lee, 2007; So and Stuphorn, 2010).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work on anatomy and function.

claim: Neuronal activity in DLPFC, ACC, and SEF is related to the expected amount or delay/proximity of rewards.
source: Especially, the dorsal part of the head of the CD (dCDh) is best situated to participate in temporal discounting processes because it receives strong convergent inputs from various frontal cortical areas including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and the supplementary eye field (SEF) (Haber et al., 1995; Haber et al., 2006), where neuronal activity is related to the expected amount or delay/proximity of rewards (Shidara and Richmond, 2002; Roesch and Olson, 2003; Roesch and Olson, 2005; Tsujimoto and Sawaguchi, 2005; Sohn and Lee, 2007; So and Stuphorn, 2010).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons in dCDh respond in relation to temporally discounted values during intertemporal choice.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that neurons in this CD sector respond in relation to temporally discounted values during intertemporal choice (Cai et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous work.

claim: It is not yet clear how dCDh contributes to the computation of motivational value with temporal discounting.
source: However, it is not yet clear how dCDh contributes to the computation of motivational value with temporal discounting.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: A subpopulation of single dCDh neurons increased their activity during the time period from the cue onset to the execution of action.
source: We found that a subpopulation of single dCDh neurons increased their activity during the time period from the cue onset to the execution of action.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The activity of many neurons was correlated with the temporally discounted value related to the expected value of outcome.
source: The activity of many neurons was correlated with the temporally discounted value related to the expected value of outcome.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The activity of dCDh neurons was not influenced by the level of satiation.
source: However, the activity was not influenced by the level of satiation.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Bilateral pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of dCDh markedly distorted the normal task performance based on the integration of reward size and delay.
source: Bilateral pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of dCDh markedly distorted the normal task performance based on the integration of reward size and delay, but did not affect the task performance for different reward sizes without delay.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Bilateral pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of dCDh did not affect the task performance for different reward sizes without delay.
source: Bilateral pharmacological or chemogenetic inactivation of dCDh markedly distorted the normal task performance based on the integration of reward size and delay, but did not affect the task performance for different reward sizes without delay.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: dCDh is involved in encoding the integrated multi-dimensional information critical for motivation.
source: These results suggest that dCDh is involved in encoding the integrated multi-dimensional information critical for motivation.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a conclusion.

claim: Neuronal activity in the dorsal part of the primate caudate head (dCDh) signals the temporally discounted value needed to compute the motivation for delayed rewards.
source: Here we show that neuronal activity in the dorsal part of the primate caudate head (dCDh) signals the temporally discounted value needed to compute the motivation for delayed rewards.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Single dCDh neurons represented the temporally discounted value without reflecting changes in the animal's physiological state.
source: Single dCDh neurons represented the temporally discounted value without reflecting changes in the animal's physiological state.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Motivation for engaging in action depends on the expected value of its outcome.
source: Motivation for engaging in action depends on the expected value of its outcome, e.g., when and how much money or food will be available as a reward.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a general principle.

claim: The larger and earlier the reward is, the greater the motivation will be.
source: Intuitively, the larger and earlier the reward is, the greater the motivation will be.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a general principle.

claim: When animals and humans suppose the reward to be delayed, their behaviors become slower and less accurate.
source: When animals and humans suppose the reward to be delayed, their behaviors become slower and less accurate.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a general observation.

claim: This decline in motivation is conceptualized as discounting of reward value as a function of time, namely temporal discounting.
source: This decline in motivation is conceptualized as discounting of reward value as a function of time, namely temporal discounting (Minamimoto et al., 2009; Shadmehr et al., 2010; Berret and Jean, 2016).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: The DV signal could not be a direct reflection of eye movements or gaze variables, since the monkeys constantly looked at the cue during the cue period regardless of the rewarding condition.
source: Although it has been reported eye movement-related activity of CD neurons modulated by forthcoming rewarding conditions (Watanabe et al., 2003), the DV signal observed here could not be a direct reflection of eye movements or gaze variables, since the monkeys constantly looked at the cue during the cue period regardless of the rewarding condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to eye tracking data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The DV signal emerged just after cue onset, gradually increased, and then disappeared before execution of the action.
source: The DV signal emerged just after cue onset, gradually increased, and then disappeared before execution of the action (Figure 5).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The neuronal signal does not simply convey the Pavlovian value of the cue, but can be related to the cognitive process mediating the outcome prediction underlying the decision of whether to act or not.
source: This time course suggests that the neuronal signal does not simply convey the Pavlovian value of the cue, but can be related to the cognitive process mediating the outcome prediction underlying the decision of whether to act or not.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the time course data.

claim: The signal integration may take place at least partially in some upstream brain area(s).
source: Compared with DV, the effect of the reward size or delay duration on cue responses was relatively weak (Figure 4), indicating that the signal integration may take place at least partially in some upstream brain area(s).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data in Figure 4.

claim: The first plausible source of temporal discounting is a prefronto-striatal projection.
source: The first plausible source of temporal discounting is a prefronto-striatal projection.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: The recordings were carried out from dCDh, the region receiving direct input from the frontal cortical areas including DLPFC, ACC, and SEF.
source: Our recordings were carried out from dCDh, the region receiving direct input from the frontal cortical areas including DLPFC, ACC, and SEF (Selemon and Goldman-Rakic, 1985; Calzavara et al., 2007; Averbeck et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous anatomical work.

claim: DLPFC neurons encode DV as well as reward, delay duration, and target position during an intertemporal choice task.
source: DLPFC neurons encode DV as well as reward, delay duration, and target position during an intertemporal choice task (Kalenscher et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2008), exhibiting strong modulations in response to the delay combined with the amount of reward (Tsujimoto and Sawaguchi, 2005; Sohn and Lee, 2007; Hosokawa et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The activity in ACC reflects the expected amount of reward and the delay/proximity of rewards, as well as delay discounting for reward.
source: The activity in ACC reflects the expected amount of reward (Knutson et al., 2005; Amiez et al., 2006) and the delay/proximity of rewards (Shidara and Richmond, 2002), as well as delay discounting for reward (McClure et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons in SEF are modulated by the amount of reward and delay duration.
source: Neurons in SEF are also modulated by the amount of reward and delay duration (Roesch and Olson, 2003; Roesch and Olson, 2005; So and Stuphorn, 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The second possible source is a nigrostriatal dopaminergic input.
source: The second possible source is a nigrostriatal dopaminergic input.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: When a stimulus signaled the timing of reward delivery, the stimulus response of dopaminergic neurons declined hyperbolically with the delay duration.
source: When a stimulus signaled the timing of reward delivery, the stimulus response of dopaminergic neurons declined hyperbolically with the delay duration (Kobayashi and Schultz, 2008).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: The third possible source is a thalamostriatal input arising from thalamic nuclei, including the centromedian-parafascicular (CM-Pf) complex.
source: The third possible source is a thalamostriatal input arising from thalamic nuclei, including the centromedian-parafascicular (CM-Pf) complex (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Neuronal activity in CM reflects the predicted outcome value.
source: Neuronal activity in CM reflects the predicted outcome value (Minamimoto et al., 2005), but at this point, there is no evidence that it is involved in delay discounting.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: At this point, there is no evidence that CM is involved in delay discounting.
source: Neuronal activity in CM reflects the predicted outcome value (Minamimoto et al., 2005), but at this point, there is no evidence that it is involved in delay discounting.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The changing motivational value was well approximated as being exponentially decreased along with reward accumulation.
source: In our task, the changing motivational value was well approximated as being exponentially decreased along with reward accumulation (Figure 6C), while the relative effect of reward size and delay on decision appeared to be constant.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The relative effect of reward size and delay on decision appeared to be constant during satiation.
source: In our task, the changing motivational value was well approximated as being exponentially decreased along with reward accumulation (Figure 6C), while the relative effect of reward size and delay on decision appeared to be constant.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: This was in good agreement with psychological concepts of motivation, in which motivational value arises from a multiplicative interaction between external stimulus and physiological state.
source: This was in good agreement with psychological concepts of motivation, in which motivational value arises from a multiplicative interaction between external stimulus and physiological state (Toates, 1986; Berridge, 2004).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Temporal discounting and reward devaluation may be two independent processes.
source: This also suggests that temporal discounting and reward devaluation may be two independent processes, one exerting a hyperbolic effect of delay duration on the reward size changing in a trial-by-trial manner, and the other slowly decreasing the motivational value of the reward in response to reward accumulation.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: dCDh may be involved in the temporal discounting process only.
source: Our data support the notion that dCDh may be involved in the former process only; DV coding in dCDh was not sensitive to changes in internal drive (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar insensitivity to satiation has been reported in terms of cue-related activity in the ventral striatum that was correlated with reward value.
source: A similar insensitivity to satiation has been reported in terms of cue-related activity in the ventral striatum that was correlated with reward value (Roesch et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Satiety-dependent changes in neuronal activity have been seen in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventromedial prefrontal cortex, rostromedial caudate nucleus (rmCD), and ventral pallidum (VP).
source: Satiety-dependent changes in neuronal activity have been seen in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Rolls et al., 1989; Critchley and Rolls, 1996; Bouret and Richmond, 2010), rostromedial caudate nucleus (rmCD), and ventral pallidum (VP) (Fujimoto et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: To formulate the motivational value for action, the physiological state or drive signal from this network may be integrated with temporal discounting in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuit, brain structures downstream from dCDh.
source: To formulate the motivational value for action, the physiological state or drive signal from this network may be integrated with temporal discounting in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuit, brain structures downstream from dCDh.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Muscimol inactivation is a standard procedure that has repeatedly been used in monkey studies.
source: Muscimol inactivation is a standard procedure that has repeatedly been used in monkey studies.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: Muscimol inactivation has major drawbacks: (1) the extent of an effective area is difficult to be controlled or identified and (2) when the experiments are repeated, mechanical damage to tissue would accumulate.
source: It has, however, major drawbacks: (1) the extent of an effective area is difficult to be controlled or identified (although we monitored the location of injection sites by computed tomography [CT]) and (2) when the experiments are repeated, mechanical damage to tissue would accumulate.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as limitations of the method.

claim: The chemogenetic tool DREADDs overcomes the problems of muscimol inactivation; once a silencing DREADDs, hM4Di, is delivered, substantially the same neuronal population can be inactivated non-invasively and the effective region can be confirmed by PET imaging and by traditional post-mortem histochemistry.
source: The chemogenetic tool DREADDs, on the other hand, overcomes these problems; once a silencing DREADDs, hM4Di, is delivered, substantially the same neuronal population can be inactivated non-invasively and the effective region can be confirmed by PET imaging, as demonstrated here, and by traditional post-mortem histochemistry.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as advantages of the method.

claim: Inactivation of dCDh by either method produced consistent behavioral impairments; inactivation abolished the normal pattern of error rates derived from the integration of reward size and delay duration.
source: We found that inactivation of dCDh by either method produced consistent behavioral impairments; inactivation abolished the normal pattern of error rates derived from the integration of reward size and delay duration (Figure 7).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 7.

claim: This impairment cannot be explained simply by changes in the temporal discounting rate or alterations in the evaluation of single incentive factors.
source: This impairment cannot be explained simply by changes in the temporal discounting rate or alterations in the evaluation of single incentive factors.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The results are consistent with previous findings that both lesioning and inactivation of the dorsomedial striatum in rats, a homologue of dCDh in primates, reduced the sensitivity of instrumental performance to shifts in the outcome value.
source: Our results are consistent with previous findings that both lesioning and inactivation of the dorsomedial striatum in rats, a homologue of dCDh in primates, reduced the sensitivity of instrumental performance to shifts in the outcome value (Yin et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: dCDh inactivation did not impair motivation based on reward size alone or according to the integration of reward size and physiological state.
source: In contrast, dCDh inactivation did not impair motivation based on reward size alone or according to the integration of reward size and physiological state (i.e., motivational value; Figure 8).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 8.

claim: The impairment can be attributed to the loss of DV coding seen in the activity of single dCDh neurons.
source: Thus, impairment can be attributed to the loss of DV coding seen in the activity of single dCDh neurons.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Similar specific impairments have also been found in monkeys with bilateral ablation of DLPFC.
source: Similar specific impairments have also been found in monkeys with bilateral ablation of DLPFC (Simmons et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Given intact motivational evaluation for the reward size alone in these cases, the motivational process appears to gain access to value signals bypassing the DLPFC-CD pathway.
source: Given intact motivational evaluation for the reward size alone in these cases, the motivational process appears to gain access to value signals bypassing the DLPFC-CD pathway.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: A plausible network for the reward size process is prefronto-basal ganglia projections from OFC to rmCD/ventral striatum and/or VP.
source: A plausible network for the reward size process is prefronto-basal ganglia projections from OFC to rmCD/ventral striatum and/or VP (Haber et al., 2006), since ablation or inactivation of these related areas abolished the normal relationship between reward size and error rate in the reward-size task (Simmons et al., 2010; Nagai et al., 2016; Fujimoto et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Ablation or inactivation of OFC, rmCD/ventral striatum, and/or VP abolished the normal relationship between reward size and error rate in the reward-size task.
source: A plausible network for the reward size process is prefronto-basal ganglia projections from OFC to rmCD/ventral striatum and/or VP (Haber et al., 2006), since ablation or inactivation of these related areas abolished the normal relationship between reward size and error rate in the reward-size task (Simmons et al., 2010; Nagai et al., 2016; Fujimoto et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The findings support the concept that incentive motivation is processed through the prefronto-basal ganglia circuit in accordance with certain topographic organization.
source: Therefore, our findings, together with our previous results, support the concept that incentive motivation is processed through the prefronto-basal ganglia circuit in accordance with certain topographic organization (Balleine et al., 2007; Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The findings provide evidence that defines a specific role of dCDh in incentive motivation, as dCDh signals the integrated multi-dimensional factors and contributes to computation of the motivational value.
source: Our findings additionally provide evidence that defines a specific role of dCDh in incentive motivation, as dCDh signals the integrated multi-dimensional factors and contributes to computation of the motivational value.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion.

claim: Dysregulation of normal temporal discounting is associated with increased impulsive behavior.
source: Our findings may also have some clinical relevance. Dysregulation of normal temporal discounting is associated with increased impulsive behavior.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as background for clinical relevance.

claim: Impulsive behavior and preference are often manifested in patients with psychiatric disorders, including depression, schizophrenia, bipolar disorders, obsessive–compulsive disorders, and substance use disorders.
source: Impulsive behavior and preference are often manifested in patients with psychiatric disorders, including depression, schizophrenia, bipolar disorders, obsessive–compulsive disorders, and substance use disorders (Pulcu et al., 2014; Amlung et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Human imaging studies have revealed the structural and functional connectivity between DLPFC and the striatum with the individual differences in temporal discounting.
source: Human imaging studies have revealed the structural and functional connectivity between DLPFC and the striatum with the individual differences in temporal discounting (van den Bos et al., 2014; van den Bos et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The findings may provide a framework to elucidate dysregulation of motivational systems in impulsive individuals with psychiatric disorders.
source: Nevertheless, our findings may provide a framework to elucidate dysregulation of motivational systems in impulsive individuals with psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as potential clinical relevance.

claim: dCDh neurons encode, at a single-neuron level, temporally discounted values of forthcoming rewards without reflecting any internal state alteration.
source: In summary, our work indicates that dCDh neurons encode, at a single-neuron level, temporally discounted values of forthcoming rewards without reflecting any internal state alteration.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary conclusion.

claim: These signals are likely to be used in downstream brain structures for formulating motivation of action especially when multi-dimensional factors have to be jointly evaluated.
source: These signals are likely to be used in downstream brain structures for formulating motivation of action especially when multi-dimensional factors have to be jointly evaluated.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary conclusion.
